newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Bock takes first Lonrho step.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Bock takes first Lonrho step.

text.p: It has taken some time, but Lonrho on Thursday finally took the first step on the road to a long-awaited three-way split by selling its Metropole hotels.

Lonrho's shares bubbled up several times late in 1995 in anticipation of a company breakup, the brainchild of departing chief executive Dieter Bock. But when it was finally announced in February this year, the stocks sank into lethargy.

The shares have slipped some 31 percent since then and eased another penny to trade at 149-1/2 on Thursday, following news that Lonrho had sold the five Metropole hotels to Britain's Stakis for 327 million pounds ($532.5 million).
In contrast, London's FTSE 100 index has risen 4.8 percent over the past nine months.
Lonrho still has to divest its Princess hotels and spin off its African trading activities before completing Bock's grand plan, and Lonrho is nothing more than its mining operations.
So, a lot still needs to be done following several earlier changes in direction and adjustments of plans.
"There have been one or two hicccups on the way," said analyst Charles Kernot at Paribas Capital Markets.
During the summer, Lonrho abandoned plans to start the demerger process by hiving off the mining business and then, decided to sell the hotels rather than float them off as a single company.
But analysts said shareholders should not complain. Bock has set out the right course, and investors should not forget that without him, there probably would not be any Lonrho at all.
The German property magnate underwrote a 1993 rights issue that rebuilt the cash-strapped conglomerate.
And shares in Lonrho have still shown an 11.2-percent rise to date since March 1995, when Bock took over from founder Tiny Rowland who was ousted after a very public power struggle.

It took Rowland 34 years to make Lonrho a firm with more than 500 units, operating in four continents. But the conglomerate would have remained secretive and opaque if its founder had stayed on, analysts said.
Consequently, it would have had a hard time finding any bank's money under Rowland. But Bock could ensure that Lonrho would shortly be in hardly any need of bankers' money at all.

If all goes according to plan and market expectations, the imminent sale of the Princess hotels in the U.S. and the Caribbean should fill Lonrho's pockets with another 340 million pounds, which, with the Metropole sale proceeds, is enough to re-pay almost all debt.
As a result, the African trading business, which will likely be floated off early in 1996, and the mining rump will have excellent balance sheets, analysts said.
So, forget the recent past and start buying Lonrho shares again, some pundits say.
"Now, there is a definite direction the company has started to walk down. The real value will come out, and I stick with a valuation of 210 pence," said Kernot.
